content:
# Workshop 7
 
 # Ask Me Anything on Inviting, Summarizing, and Responding to Public Comments
 
 **Speakers:** [Michael A. Livermore](https:/www.law.virginia.edu/faculty/profile/mal5un/2457619) (Professor of Law, University of Virginia School of Law), [Alex Spangher](https:/profiles.stanford.edu/alexander-spangher) (Postdoctoral Scholar, Stanford University), [Bill Zipse](https:/www.linkedin.com/in/william-zipse-0ba94773) (Supervising Forester, New Jersey Forest Service)
 
 Government agencies routinely face capacity constraints in collecting public input. They solicit comments on planning decisions, proposed rules, and policy changes, then struggle to process them in time to inform the decisions those comments are meant to shape. The typical response is either to dedicate staff for months of manual review or to treat the comment period as a compliance formality rather than a genuine source of information. This workshop asked what practitioners can do now, without multi-year platform development or dedicated engineering teams.
 
 Other sessions in the series showcase custom-built systems — Hamburg's [](https:/dipas.org) [DIPAS platform](https:/dipas.org) , Bowling Green's partnership with [](https:/jigsaw.google.com) [Google Jigsaw](https:/jigsaw.google.com) — that required substantial investment. This workshop inverted the premise by focusing on commercially available tools and basic scripting, discussing what's safe to try and what actually works.
 
 The panel combined a practitioner who had experimented with AI comment analysis (Bill Zipse, New Jersey Forest Service) with two researchers who study computational approaches to public input (Michael Livermore at UVA Law, Alex Spangher at Stanford's RegLab).
 
 ## Three months to thirty-six hours
 
 The session's anchor was Zipse's work on two New Jersey projects. At [](https:/www.nj.gov/dep/parksandforests/parks/libertystatepark.html) [Liberty State Park](https:/www.nj.gov/dep/parksandforests/parks/libertystatepark.html) — the departure point for the Statue of Liberty ferry — the state had collected thousands of comments on proposed development projects. Staff had manually reviewed in-person comment cards, but online submissions were backlogged. With a public meeting approaching, the administration wanted a synopsis. The original estimate for manual review was three months.
 
 Zipse's team, which normally handles biometric analysis for forest management, used GPT-3.5, Python (Pandas, NumPy, SciPy), and the OpenAI API to process the comments in roughly 36 hours. They worked in two modes: iterating through a spreadsheet to classify individual comments, and vectorizing batches of anonymized comments for summarization. All personally identifiable information was stripped using local scripts before any AI processing.
 
 That compression — three months to a day and a half — is the headline. But the project also exposed limits. Sentiment analysis achieved only about 60% accuracy, barely better than chance. The model couldn't handle sarcasm: "'Oh yeah, I can't believe they're putting this in the train station, that's a great idea!' Well, that's not a positive comment." A developer named Fireman caused a different error when the model concluded residents had strong opinions about the fire department. And crucially, the team's ability to validate results depended on having manually reviewed comment cards as training data.
 
 A second project at [Wharton State Forest](https:/dep.nj.gov/parksandforests/state-park/wharton-state-forest) offered a contrasting case. The Pine Barrens' sand roads have accumulated multiple colloquial names over generations; the task was to extract road names from unstructured comments and join them to a GIS database. This worked well precisely because it was constrained — entity extraction rather than meaning extraction, pulling out specific terms rather than interpreting sentiment. "The more specific and bounded the task," Zipse said, "the more reliable the output."
 
 ## 
 
 ## What AI can and cannot do
 
 Livermore framed the discussion with a constraint that shaped the rest of the session: "What you can't do, which would be awesome, is go to ChatGPT, give it all of your comments, and say, 'tell me what is useful in these comments.' That you can't do. The technology isn't even remotely there." The tools function as sieves — they help process volume — but the judgment about what matters remains with the human operator.
 
 The reliable uses share a pattern: they're specific, bounded, and don't require the model to exercise judgment about meaning.
 
 **Deduplication** is the clearest example. Mass comment campaigns generate thousands of identical submissions; you want to count them but don't need to read them a thousand times. Finding exact matches is trivial; finding near-duplicates (90% similar) requires embedding-based tools but remains straightforward.
 
 **Topic modeling** provides a bird's-eye view without predefined categories. Spangher, who used topic modeling at the New York Times to track reader complaints, recommends it because "it's cheap, it runs on your computer, you don't share data with the cloud, and there's a lot of theory that backs it up." The algorithm discovers themes by looking at which words appear together; you don't tell it what to find.
 
 Livermore also introduced " **featurization** "— converting messy comments into structured data by defining features in advance. Does the commenter support the proposal? Raise environmental concerns? Claim expertise? You run each comment through an LLM with prompts for each question, and the output is stored in a database. If the model is cheap, run each comment through thirty times for thirty features. The constraint — human-defined categories applied at scale — is what makes it reliable.
 
 **Prioritization** asks which comments deserve attention first. Spangher's Stanford lab, working with [](https:/law.stanford.edu/directory/daniel-e-ho) [Daniel Ho](https:/law.stanford.edu/directory/daniel-e-ho) , has built routing pipelines for the EPA and a Chilean regulatory agency. Livermore proposed a simpler version: prompt the model to rate each comment 0-10 on the likelihood of containing new information, validate against a hand-coded sample, then triage from the top.
 
 **At the bottom of the reliability hierarchy are open-ended tasks** : sentiment analysis and unconstrained summarization. A related problem Zipse noted: LLMs may over-weight unusual comments because distinctive language stands out. If 10,000 people send a form letter and two write something idiosyncratic, the model may focus on the outliers.
 
 ## The expertise problem
 
 There's a tension in how public comment processes are understood. One view treats comments as votes: the goal is to gauge public sentiment, and the relevant question is whether people support or oppose a proposal. A second view treats comments as sources of information: the goal is to surface knowledge the decision-maker doesn't have — technical expertise from engineers, on-the-ground experience from affected communities, economic analysis from industry, scientific evidence from researchers. **Noveck called this distinction "sentiment versus expertise elicitation."**
 
 Current AI tools are substantially better at the first task than the second. Sentiment classification is "the easiest task for AI" — if all the model has to return is thumbs up or thumbs down, it can achieve reasonable accuracy (though NJ's 60% figure suggests even this is fragile). Detecting whether a comment contains substantively new information is much harder.
 
 **The distinction matters because, especially in rulemaking contexts, sentiment is often the least valuable output.** Federal rulemaking comments become part of the litigation record; courts scrutinize how agencies handled substantive objections, not how many people clicked "oppose." Rules attract comments from engineers, economists, and industry groups whose specialized knowledge may be relevant to decision-making. The challenge is identifying which comments contain that knowledge — precisely the task current tools handle poorly.
 
 ## 
 
 ## The prompt problem
 
 Spangher emphasized a structural challenge that practitioners often miss: **models update constantly, fine-tuned by providers in ways users don't observe.** "Every time these models update, their behavior does change. They're constantly being fine-tuned to be more helpful in the way OpenAI decides is more helpful... just because your golden prompt worked with GPT-4.0 doesn't mean it will necessarily work with GPT-5, or the next update of GPT-5 that happens under the hood."
 
 His practical recommendation: hand-annotate 100 comments to create a benchmark set. This takes hours, not weeks, and provides ground truth to test against when model behavior shifts. For rare-class detection — finding "needles in haystacks" — you may need to write synthetic examples of what you're looking for, since rare classes by definition don't appear often in real data. Spangher's team did this when searching for discriminatory provisions in state law. Tools like [](https:/dspy.ai) [DSPy](https:/dspy.ai) can help with automatic prompt optimization, though Spangher noted it remains experimental. "If there's one thing I could leave you with," he concluded, "it's just benchmark more, and don't assume that your prompt today is gonna work tomorrow."
 
 ## Looking forward
 
 Spangher raised a provocation about AI-mediated participation. His lab is building tools that work the opposite direction from comment analysis: helping non-industry groups write comments that agencies will consider. Many academics have relevant expertise but don't know the genre conventions. The SEC, for instance, will only consider comments that include cost-benefit analysis — a format most researchers don't naturally produce. Tools that help experts frame input in agency-legible terms could shift who participates effectively. "It's kind of funny," Spangher noted, "because we were talking on both sides — what are tools to get more people to comment, and then what are tools to get agencies to digest comments — and there's kind of a 'my bot is talking to your bot' scenario happening."
 
 Livermore proposed two additional directions. First, using AI on the front end to help citizens understand complex rulemakings before they comment — a 200-page rule is illegible to most people, and an interactive tool explaining what the agency wants to know could generate more useful input. Second, creating lateral deliberation among commenters rather than the current unidirectional flow. Other jurisdictions experiment with deliberative processes; AI tools might enable this at scale.
 
 Zipse's framing was immediate: AI enables responsiveness. The bottleneck was always processing capacity. If you can analyze comments in a day instead of three months, you can actually incorporate public input into decisions. "For me, the future is a much more interactive and responsive government where what the public is concerned about matters, where it can be heard and applied much more efficiently."
 
 ## Implications for practice
 
 Zipse's advice for getting started: "Pick something where you already have publicly available data... take as little risk as possible in the beginning, and give yourself room to fail." Experiment with data that's already public. If you have any manually-reviewed comments to validate against, use them. Tools like [](https:/notebooklm.google) [Google Notebook LM](https:/notebooklm.google) can provide quick document summaries and mind-mapping, though Zipse cautioned to stay alert for what might be missing.
 
 The core lesson is that AI tools should be understood as a hierarchy ordered by reliability. At the top: bounded-extraction tasks such as deduplication and entity extraction. In the middle: discovery techniques like topic modeling and classification via featurization. At the bottom: open-ended interpretation, like sentiment analysis and summarization. Agencies should match their ambitions to this hierarchy, starting with tasks where failure is recoverable and validation is straightforward.
 
 ## Quotes
 
 ### Bill Zipse (NJ Forest Service)
 
 “We’re kind of short-staffed, like a lot of government agencies, and it’s a big job trying to vet the diverse opinions in New Jersey.”
 
 “In about a day and a half, we had a pretty good idea of what those comments contained.”
 
 “It’s not AI making the decision, but bringing something to your attention, and you can get that in front of somebody who knows about that subject.”
 
 “My advice is I’d pick something where you already have publicly available data… take as little risk as possible in the beginning, and give yourself room to fail.”
 
 “Sometimes it almost feels like some of the minority comments rose to the surface pretty quickly. So you kind of have to balance what’s repeated over and over with unique material.”
 
 “I would like to lean into the ability of these tools to democratize and be more responsive.”
 
 ### Michael A. Livermore (University of Virginia)
 
 “The problem with comments is that there’s just so much. You’re trying to toke this firehose of information and narrow it down.”
 
 “What you can’t do is go to ChatGPT, give it all your comments, and say, ‘Hey, tell me what is useful in these comments.’ The technology isn’t even remotely there to do that.”
 
 “It’s almost irreplaceable work, saying ‘what information do I want?’ and then ‘what can I start to offload to these tools?’”
 
 “Have your LLM assess the likelihood that this comment has new information for you from 0 to 10 as a way of prioritizing your efforts.”
 
 ### Alexander Spangher
 
 “If you’re gonna use LLMs with summarization or anything, I would really pay attention to benchmarks that exist.”
 
 “Topic modeling… it’s cheap, it runs on your computer, you don’t share data with the cloud.”
 
 “We say summarization a lot, but priortization is also a very important way of getting a sense of what the public is saying.”
 
 “Before you deploy any of these tools, think about what the ideal inputs and outputs are going to be.”
 
 “Just because your golden prompt worked for GPT-4.0 doesn’t mean it will necessarily work for 5, or the next update.”
 
 ## 
 
 ## Audience notes
 
 ### Questions
 
 "What does vectorizing for the LLM mean?"
 
 "Have you found the AI tools tease out topics if the view of the planner or analyst is looking for a needle-in-the-haystack type of input?"
 
 "Do you do custom scripts that reflect what you're looking for from the comments or do you use Python APIs?"
 
 Are there ways to interactively categorize comments, and then review those categories to adjust them if you think something should have multiple tags/categories or is in the wrong spot? Ideally in some kind of Excel/Airtable format."
 
 "You mentioned determining WHO made a comment — how have you addressed anonymity in comment collection?"
 
 "Is there something to which an interested citizen can point... in order to prod a government agency to explore the idea of AI for summarization?"
 
 "How do I find more training or information on safeguarding virtual meeting information related to AI? My agency is running into problems with AI chatbot summaries being generated after virtual meetings and sometimes being inaccurate."
 
 "Could you please add the link to the tool you suggest for newsworthiness prioritization?"
 
 ### Reasons for attending
 
 77% to get familiar with new AI tools/technologies for engagement, 56% to learn new skills/techniques, 48% to increase confidence using these tools, 46% to build confidence in creating public value (trust, responsiveness, transparency, efficiency, inclusion), 27% to hear from specific instructors/experts, 15% to network with peers, 4% other.
 
 ### Top challenges in online public engagement
 
 ### 
 
 48% limited technical skills or confidence with digital tools, 44% lack of time or staff capacity, 40% low public trust/transparency/credibility of the process, 29% limited organizational support or leadership buy-in, 25% difficulty reaching diverse or representative audiences, 23% challenges in moderating or managing online discussions, 23% budget or funding constraints, 21% difficulty demonstrating impact or value of engagement outcomes.
 
 ### 
 
 ### Participants
 
 The session drew heavy representation from New Jersey state government: Lisa Schaefer (NJ DEP, stormwater, Trenton), Ben Trotter (NJ DEP, Wharton State Forest/State Park Service), Nathaly Agosto Filion (NJ DEP Office of Climate Resilience), Marsinette Nelson (State of New Jersey), and multiple other NJ DEP staff. Other government participants included Davyd Smith (IT Director, State of Colorado), Ronald Aleteanu (Small Business/Title VI Manager, California High-Speed Rail Authority, Sacramento), and Ben Peterson (Executive Director, Bowling Green City-County Planning Commission, Kentucky). Academic participants included Sowmini Sengupta (doctoral student, Portland State University, researching sensemaking and AI in public opinion for infrastructure planning). International participants joined from Budapest, Hungary (Pálfy Katalin, local ecosystem development and infrastructure funds), Sweden (Magnus M Larsen, nature/social design), Romania (Raluca Onufreiciuc), Rio de Janeiro (Mauricio Ribeiro), and Baja California, Mexico (César Loustaunau, Agencia Digital de Baja California). US participants also joined from Washington DC, Tucson AZ, San Antonio TX, Montgomery County MD (Nikki Smallwood, Christina Lottie, Woody Campbell, Josh Cole), Cambridge MA, Loveland CO, Albany NY, Harrisburg PA, and Orlando FL.

 ## Resources
 
 [Gensim LDA Tutorial](https:/radimrehurek.com/gensim/auto_examples/tutorials/run_lda.html) — Standard implementation of Latent Dirichlet Allocation for topic discovery
 
 [NYT Recommendation Engine](https:/archive.nytimes.com/open.blogs.nytimes.com/2015/08/11/building-the-next-new-york-times-recommendation-engine) — How the Times used topic modeling at scale (referenced by Spangher)
 
 [LLMs + Topic Modeling (2024 paper)](https:/www.arxiv.org/pdf/2505.23166) — Recent research combining large language models with topic modeling approaches
 
 [OpenAI Embeddings Guide](https:/platform.openai.com/docs/guides/embeddings) — Official documentation on text embeddings for similarity and clustering
 
 [Scikit-learn Clustering](https:/scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html) — Python library documentation for clustering algorithms
 
 [Cohere Clustering Tutorial](https:/cohere.com/llmu/clustering-with-embeddings) — End-to-end tutorial combining embeddings with clustering (shared by Spangher)
 
 [EPA Comment Prioritization (Ho et al., Stanford RegLab)](https:/aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.1788.pdf) — Research paper on AI-assisted routing for regulatory comments
 
 [Newsworthiness Detection in City Council Meetings (Spangher)](https:/arxiv.org/pdf/2311.09734) — Related work on prioritizing content in public proceedings
 
 [GEM Benchmark](https:/gem-benchmark.com) — Environment for natural language generation evaluation (shared by Spangher)
 
 [Summarization Model Leaderboard](https:/www.prollm.ai/leaderboard/summarization) — Comparative rankings of summarization models
 
 [DSPy](https:/dspy.ai) — Framework for automatic prompt optimization (noted as experimental by Spangher)
 
 [Google Notebook LM](https:/notebooklm.google) — Document summarization and mind-mapping tool (mentioned by Zipse)
 
 [Liberty State Park](https:/www.nj.gov/dep/parksandforests/parks/libertystatepark.html) — Primary case study site
 
 [Hamburg DIPAS Platform](https:/dipas.org) — Custom comment analysis system (referenced as contrast case)
 
 [Regulations.gov](https:/www.regulations.gov) — Federal rulemaking comment database (source for practice datasets)
